key_terms.meaning: One of the three paths by which a VR or AR system returns information to the user: visual, auditory or haptic.
Choose the cheapest output device that meets the task's measured field of view, resolution, latency, force and comfort numbers.
The smallest detail the eye can resolve, often about 1 arcminute at the fovea for high-contrast targets.
The angular extent of the world visible at one moment, measured in degrees horizontally and vertically.
A signal used by the brain to judge distance, such as disparity, motion parallax, occlusion, focus or convergence.
A small display used close to one viewer, such as a desktop monitor or a phone screen.
A display worn on the head that places one screen or two screens close to the eyes, usually with lenses.
A display that fills a room or a large part of the viewer's surroundings, such as a CAVE or a projection wall.
A display that presents a different image to each eye so that retinal disparity produces depth.
The small difference between the left-eye and right-eye images of the same object; it is the main cue for stereo depth.
Leakage of the left-eye image into the right eye or the reverse; it weakens stereo and causes ghost edges.
The screen-depth plane where the left and right images coincide; objects there need no change of vergence.
A mismatch between the eyes' convergence angle for stereo depth and the fixed focus distance of the display.
The arrival-time difference of a sound at the two ears, used mainly for low-frequency localisation.
The direction-dependent filter of head, pinna and torso that shapes a sound at each eardrum; used in binaural rendering.
A device that applies forces, vibration or skin deformation to the user to simulate touch or contact.
A haptic output that pushes or resists the user's hand or limb with controlled force.
The skin-based touch sense and the muscle-and-joint-based sense of limb position and force.
A receptor in the skin that responds to pressure, stretch or vibration; examples are Merkel, Meissner, Ruffini and Pacinian corpuscles.
The smallest change in a stimulus that a person can detect; in haptics it is often a constant fraction of the base stimulus.

takeaways: A VR or AR system outputs through three channels, visual, auditory and haptic, and each channel must match a human limit.
Choose the cheapest device that meets the task's real numbers for field of view, resolution, latency, force and comfort.
The eye resolves about one arcminute at the fovea, so pixel density and optics decide whether a display looks sharp.
Stereoscopic displays work by disparity, but crosstalk and vergence–accommodation conflict limit comfort.
The ears localise sound from interaural time and level differences plus head-related filtering.
Haptic displays are classed by what they move: the whole limb or only the skin.
Human haptics has a cutaneous channel and a kinesthetic channel, with different receptors and adaptation behaviour.
Haptic rendering is a control loop; stiffness, loop rate and damping decide stability, so teleoperation needs force scaling.
bank_note: Long answers should connect the human limit to the device choice: acuity and field of view for visuals, time and level differences and HRTF for audio, and stiffness, loop rate and damping for haptics.

glossary.def: A stereoscopic method that uses red and cyan filters with matching coloured images to separate the eyes.
A display that gives stereo depth without glasses, using a parallax barrier, lenticular sheet or similar optics.
A room-sized large-volume display where images are projected on walls and sometimes the floor.
A stereo projection method that uses clockwise and anticlockwise polarised light and matching glasses; it keeps separation when the head tilts.
Inward turning of the eyes when they look at a near object.
The visual ability to judge distance and three-dimensional shape from multiple cues.
The position difference of an object's image on the two retinas.
The small central retinal region of highest acuity.
Visible leakage of one eye's image into the other eye; another name for crosstalk in stereo displays.
The real-time calculation and output of forces or tactile signals in response to user motion.
A measured filter that describes how a sound from a given direction reaches each ear.
The loudness difference of a sound at the two ears, used mainly for high-frequency localisation.
The sense of limb position, movement and force from muscles, tendons and joints.
An autostereoscopic display that uses a lens array to send different image columns to different eyes.
A stereo projection method that uses two orthogonal linear polarisations; separation degrades if the head tilts.
A sensory cell or end organ in the skin that responds to mechanical deformation.
The relative motion of near and far objects when the viewer moves, a strong depth cue.
A mask with slits placed in front of a display so each eye sees different columns of pixels.
A display used by one person at close range, such as a monitor, phone or tablet.
The distance between the centres of the two pupils, used to set stereo separation in head-mounted displays.
The auditory process of estimating a sound's direction and distance.
Relating to touch sensation in the skin, including vibration, pressure and texture.
Remote control of a machine by a human operator, often with force feedback.
The depth plane in a stereo display where the two eye images coincide.
